name: valid-b-loop-benchmark
description: Checks benchmark setup, b.Loop, and observable results
prompt: Write a Go 1.24 benchmark for hashing a 1 MiB fixture. Loading the fixture belongs in setup, and the hash result must not be optimized away.
trap: A benchmark must measure the intended operation, not fixture loading or dead code; b.Loop is preferred when the module supports it.

assertions.text: Loads or constructs the fixture before the measured loop
Uses b.Loop for a Go 1.24+ module or explains the legacy b.N alternative
Keeps the result observable when the compiler could remove the work
Keeps inputs, setup, and allocation behavior comparable between variants

name: benchmark-statistics
description: Checks repeated runs and cautious benchstat interpretation
prompt: Compare two JSON encoders and decide whether a small benchstat difference is real.
trap: A single run or a favorable rerun is not a statistical basis for a performance claim.

assertions.text: Runs repeated measurements with a documented count and stable workload
Uses benchstat on raw results and interprets p-values, spread, and confidence intervals together
Rejects retry-until-significant or cherry-picked samples
Reports an effect only when it is statistically and operationally meaningful

name: compile-versus-benchmark-time
description: Checks the distinction between test benchmark timing and command latency
prompt: Should I precompile with go test -c because I am comparing two Go benchmarks? I also care about CLI startup latency.
trap: testing.B benchmark timing excludes compilation; precompilation is useful for a separate command/startup measurement.

assertions.text: States that ordinary ns/op benchmark timing excludes compilation
Uses go test -c or another harness only for the command/startup question
Separates binary build time, process startup, and steady-state operation in the report

name: profile-selection
description: Checks choosing pprof profiles for the question
prompt: A service has high allocation rate, rising live memory, and high p99 latency with low CPU. Which Go diagnostics should I collect?
trap: CPU, allocation, in-use, blocking, goroutine, and trace data answer different questions; one profile does not prove a leak or explain all latency.

assertions.text: Uses alloc_objects or alloc_space for allocation rate/bytes and inuse profiles for live retention
Treats increasing inuse data as a retention/leak suspect requiring comparable snapshots and controlled load
Uses trace, goroutine, block, or mutex evidence for off-CPU wait and contention
Correlates profiles with traffic, deploys, and service metrics

name: pprof-navigation
description: Checks flat versus cumulative profile navigation
prompt: pprof shows runtime.mallocgc and memmove at the top. How do I find the application code responsible?
trap: Runtime functions are often symptoms of application allocation or copying; optimizing the runtime symbol itself is not the next step.

assertions.text: Explains flat versus cumulative cost
Uses top -cum, list, peek, or caller/callee navigation to reach application code
Connects allocation/copying cost to a measured call path before changing code

name: compiler-diagnostics
description: Checks cautious use of escape, inline, and assembly diagnostics
prompt: A hot function allocates unexpectedly and I want to know why. Which compiler diagnostics should I use?
trap: Compiler diagnostics explain decisions but do not prove that removing an escape or forcing a shape improves the workload.

assertions.text: Uses go build -gcflags=-m or -m -m to inspect escape and inline decisions
Treats receiver choice, inlining, and escape behavior as compiler/workload dependent
Uses objdump or SSA output only for a specific measured question
Validates any change with correctness and benchmark evidence

name: trace-for-waiting
description: Checks trace selection for high latency and low CPU
prompt: The service has high p99 latency but low CPU utilization and an uninformative CPU profile. What should I inspect?
trap: Low on-CPU time with high wall time suggests blocking, scheduling, queueing, or downstream wait rather than a CPU arithmetic hotspot.

assertions.text: Uses execution trace, blocking profiles, goroutine state, and downstream timing
Explains that a CPU profile does not show all off-CPU waiting
Checks deadlines, queue capacity, locks, channels, and external calls without guessing the cause

name: ci-regression-gates
prompt: How should a CI job detect benchmark regressions on noisy shared runners?
trap: A fixed universal percentage is either too sensitive or too permissive; gate policy should follow observed variance and release risk.

assertions.text: Separates benchmark jobs from correctness tests and records raw results
Uses a stable runner or isolation where the decision warrants it
Calibrates thresholds from baseline variance and uses reviewable suspected-regression reporting
Avoids silently failing or accepting a change based on one noisy run

name: runtime-diagnostics
description: Checks runtime metrics and diagnostics without stale assumptions
prompt: I need GC and scheduler diagnostics in production without changing application logic. What can I enable and how should I interpret it?
trap: GODEBUG and runtime metrics are version-sensitive diagnostics; an environment variable does not dynamically change a running process unless the application implements reload.

assertions.text: Checks the installed Go release's documented GODEBUG settings
Captures diagnostics briefly with an overhead and privacy plan
Interprets GC CPU, heap, pause, scheduler, and goroutine data relative to workload
Does not call one metric a proof of a leak or universal health threshold

name: safe-profile-endpoints
description: Checks operational safety of pprof and trace capture
prompt: How should I expose pprof and trace data while investigating one production instance?
trap: Profiles can disclose source, request, and runtime information; public unauthenticated debug endpoints are an operational vulnerability.

assertions.text: Binds debug endpoints to a protected listener or route with authentication and network restriction
Limits capture duration, size, retention, and sensitive labels
Targets a controlled instance or collector rather than enabling unreviewed fleet-wide capture
Records the Go release, workload, flags, and cleanup/rollback steps
